title: PostgreSQL JSONB & Advanced Queries
description: Working with JSONB data type, advanced query techniques and PostgreSQL-specific features

questions.title: What is the difference between JSON and JSONB in PostgreSQL?

sections.content:
## JSON vs JSONB in PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL provides two JSON data types with very different storage and query behaviour.

**JSON** stores the raw text of the JSON input, preserving whitespace, duplicate keys, and key order. Every time you query it, PostgreSQL must re-parse the text — so reads are slower.

**JSONB** stores JSON in a decomposed binary format. Key order is not preserved, duplicate keys are removed (last value wins), but it is **pre-parsed** so reads are much faster and it supports **GIN indexing**.

### Comparison

| Feature | JSON | JSONB |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | Exact text | Binary decomposed |
| Write speed | Faster | Slightly slower |
| Read speed | Slower (re-parses) | Faster |
| Indexing | No GIN support | Full GIN support |
| Key order | Preserved | Not preserved |
| Duplicate keys | Preserved | Last value wins |

### When to use which
- **JSONB** — almost always. Better for querying, filtering, and indexing.
- **JSON** — only if you need to preserve exact input format (e.g., audit logs where whitespace matters).

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  attributes JSONB  -- use JSONB for queryability
);

INSERT INTO products (attributes) VALUES
  ('{"color": "red", "size": "M", "tags": ["sale", "new"]}');

-- Query a JSONB field
SELECT * FROM products WHERE attributes->>'color' = 'red';

-- GIN index for fast JSONB lookups
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs ON products USING GIN (attributes);
```

**Rule of thumb:** Always use JSONB unless you have a specific reason not to.

- JSONB is binary-stored and pre-parsed — reads are faster
- JSONB supports GIN indexes enabling fast containment queries
- JSON preserves input exactly; JSONB normalises (drops duplicates, reorders)
- Use `->>` for text output and `->` for JSON output when querying

questions.title: What are the key JSONB operators and how do you use them?

sections.content:
## JSONB Operators in PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL provides rich operators for querying and manipulating JSONB data.

### Extraction Operators

```sql
-- -> returns JSON (preserves type)
SELECT attributes -> 'color' FROM products;  -- returns "red" (JSON string)

-- ->> returns TEXT
SELECT attributes ->> 'color' FROM products;  -- returns red (text)

-- #> path operator (nested)
SELECT attributes #> '{address,city}' FROM users;

-- #>> path as text
SELECT attributes #>> '{address,city}' FROM users;
```

### Containment Operators

```sql
-- @> contains (left contains right)
SELECT * FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red"}';

-- <@ is contained by
SELECT * FROM products WHERE '{"color": "red"}' <@ attributes;

-- ? key exists
SELECT * FROM products WHERE attributes ? 'size';

-- ?| any of these keys exist
SELECT * FROM products WHERE attributes ?| ARRAY['size', 'weight'];

-- ?& all keys exist
SELECT * FROM products WHERE attributes ?& ARRAY['color', 'size'];
```

### Modification Operators

```sql
-- || concatenate/merge
UPDATE products
SET attributes = attributes || '{"weight": "200g"}'
WHERE id = 1;

-- - delete key
UPDATE products
SET attributes = attributes - 'old_field'
WHERE id = 1;

-- #- delete nested path
UPDATE products
SET attributes = attributes #- '{address,old_city}';
```

### Practical Query Examples

```sql
-- Find products with 'sale' tag in array
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE attributes -> 'tags' @> '["sale"]';

-- Filter and extract
SELECT
  id,
  attributes ->> 'color' AS color,
  (attributes ->> 'price')::numeric AS price
FROM products
WHERE (attributes ->> 'price')::numeric > 100;
```

- `->` returns JSON, `->>` returns text — cast explicitly for numeric comparisons
- `@>` containment with GIN index gives fast lookups on JSONB fields
- `?` checks key existence; useful for optional attribute filtering
- `||` merges two JSONB objects — great for partial updates without rewriting full JSON

questions.title: How do you index JSONB columns for optimal query performance?

sections.content:
## Indexing JSONB in PostgreSQL

Without indexes, JSONB queries do full table scans. PostgreSQL offers several index types for JSONB.

### GIN Index (General Inverted Index)

Best for containment (`@>`) and key-existence (`?`) queries.

```sql
-- Full GIN index — indexes all keys and values
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs ON products USING GIN (attributes);

-- Containment query uses the index
SELECT * FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red"}';

-- Key existence uses the index
SELECT * FROM products WHERE attributes ? 'discount';
```

### GIN with jsonb_path_ops (Smaller, Faster for @>)

```sql
-- jsonb_path_ops only supports @>, but is smaller and faster
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs_path
  ON products USING GIN (attributes jsonb_path_ops);
```

### B-tree Index on Extracted Value

Best for equality/range queries on a specific field.

```sql
-- Index on a specific extracted field
CREATE INDEX idx_products_color
  ON products ((attributes ->> 'color'));

-- Partial index — only index active products
CREATE INDEX idx_active_products_price
  ON products ((attributes ->> 'price')::numeric)
  WHERE attributes ->> 'status' = 'active';

-- Range query uses the B-tree index
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE (attributes ->> 'price')::numeric BETWEEN 10 AND 100;
```

### Choosing the Right Index

| Query Pattern | Index Type |
|---|---|
| `@>` containment | GIN (jsonb_path_ops) |
| `?` key existence | GIN (default) |
| `->>` equality on specific field | B-tree expression index |
| `->>` range on specific field | B-tree expression index |

### Performance Tip

For frequently queried specific fields, a B-tree expression index is usually faster than GIN. Use GIN when queries are dynamic and you don't know which fields will be searched.

- GIN indexes are the default choice for general JSONB query patterns
- `jsonb_path_ops` reduces GIN index size by 20-30% at the cost of only supporting `@>`
- B-tree expression indexes on extracted values are fastest for equality/range on known fields
- Always `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to verify index usage — PostgreSQL may still seq-scan for low selectivity

- Always define `columnDefinition = "jsonb"` so Hibernate creates the right column type
- Use native `@Query` for JSONB operators — JPQL/Criteria doesn't support them
- GIN index in Flyway migration ensures queries are fast from day one

questions.title: How do window functions work in PostgreSQL and when should you use them?

sections.content:
## Window Functions in PostgreSQL

Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does. They are one of the most powerful SQL features for analytics.

### Syntax

```sql
function_name() OVER (
  [PARTITION BY column]
  [ORDER BY column]
  [ROWS/RANGE frame_spec]
)
```

### Common Window Functions

```sql
-- ROW_NUMBER — unique sequential number per partition
SELECT
  employee_id,
  department,
  salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank_in_dept
FROM employees;

-- RANK vs DENSE_RANK
-- RANK skips numbers on ties; DENSE_RANK does not
SELECT
  name, score,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM scores;

-- Running total
SELECT
  order_date,
  amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM orders;

-- Moving average (last 7 days)
SELECT
  sale_date,
  daily_sales,
  AVG(daily_sales) OVER (
    ORDER BY sale_date
    ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS moving_avg_7d
FROM daily_sales;

-- LAG/LEAD — access previous/next row values
SELECT
  sale_date,
  amount,
  LAG(amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS prev_day,
  amount - LAG(amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS day_over_day_change
FROM daily_sales;
```

### Top-N per Group (common pattern)

```sql
-- Get top 3 earners per department
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT
    name, department, salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
  FROM employees
) ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;
```

### When to Use Window Functions
- Running totals, cumulative sums
- Rankings within groups
- Comparing a row to its neighbours (LAG/LEAD)
- Percentiles and distribution analysis
- Deduplication (ROW_NUMBER to find first/last per group)

- Window functions compute over a set of rows without collapsing them — unlike GROUP BY
- `PARTITION BY` defines the window groups; `ORDER BY` defines order within the window
- `ROW_NUMBER()` is the standard deduplication tool; `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` handle ties differently
- `LAG`/`LEAD` are essential for time-series comparisons and trend detection

questions.title: What are CTEs and recursive CTEs in PostgreSQL?

sections.content:
## CTEs and Recursive CTEs in PostgreSQL

### Regular CTEs (Common Table Expressions)

CTEs are named temporary result sets scoped to a single query. They improve readability and can be referenced multiple times.

```sql
-- Regular CTE
WITH active_users AS (
  SELECT id, name, email
  FROM users
  WHERE status = 'active' AND last_login > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
),
high_value_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days'
  GROUP BY user_id
  HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000
)
SELECT
  u.name,
  u.email,
  o.total AS order_total
FROM active_users u
JOIN high_value_orders o ON u.id = o.user_id;
```

### Recursive CTEs

Recursive CTEs are used to query hierarchical or graph-like data — organisational charts, category trees, bill of materials.

```sql
-- Recursive CTE: traverse an org chart
WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS (
  -- Base case: start from the top-level manager
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS level
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL

  UNION ALL

  -- Recursive step: find direct reports
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, ot.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org_tree ot ON e.manager_id = ot.id
)
SELECT
  REPEAT('  ', level) || name AS org_chart,
  level
FROM org_tree
ORDER BY level, name;

-- Category tree (self-referential)
WITH RECURSIVE category_path AS (
  SELECT id, name, parent_id, name::text AS path
  FROM categories
  WHERE parent_id IS NULL

  UNION ALL

  SELECT c.id, c.name, c.parent_id,
         cp.path || ' > ' || c.name
  FROM categories c
  JOIN category_path cp ON c.parent_id = cp.id
)
SELECT * FROM category_path ORDER BY path;
```

### Materialised CTEs (PostgreSQL 12+)

In PostgreSQL 12+, CTEs are non-materialised by default (inlined as subqueries). Use `MATERIALIZED` to force evaluation once.

```sql
WITH MATERIALIZED expensive_calc AS (
  SELECT user_id, complex_aggregation()
  FROM large_table
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT * FROM expensive_calc WHERE user_id = 42;
```

### When to Use CTEs
- Breaking complex queries into readable steps
- Reusing a subquery result multiple times
- Recursive/hierarchical queries (only CTEs support `RECURSIVE`)
- Inserting/updating with a result set (`WITH ... INSERT INTO`)

- CTEs are named result sets scoped to one query — they dramatically improve readability
- Recursive CTEs require a base case + recursive step joined by `UNION ALL`
- PostgreSQL 12+ inlines CTEs by default; add `MATERIALIZED` to force single evaluation
- Always add a cycle-detection guard (`WHERE level < 100`) in recursive CTEs to prevent infinite loops
